source: Ragni and Johnson-Laird (2020) Explanation or Modeling: a Reply to Kellen and Klauer
finding: A meta-analysis of 228 selection-task experiments (Ragni et al. 2018) supports the original model theory. Only four selections occur more often than chance: p+q, p alone, p+q+not-q (partial insight), and p+not-q (correct). The model theory survived; all but one of 15 rival theories were refuted.
numbers: 228 experiments. First four studies: p+q 46%, p 33%, p+q+not-q 7%, p+not-q 4%; the other ~10% of selections were each below chance (1/16 = 6.25%). 89 face-to-face experiments (4,230 people) vs 10 online (3,787 people).
limits: This is the authors' own reply in a dispute, so it is partisan. Kellen and Klauer dispute identifiability and the fit statistics. Only the reply was read, not the 2018 paper or the critique.
agent_relevance: The abstract task has a stable, small set of answers, and the correct one is rare. Do not expect a plain prompt to reach the falsifying test by default.

source: Ragni and Johnson-Laird (2020) Explanation or Modeling: a Reply to Kellen and Klauer
finding: Selections are dependent on one another. The informativeness (Shannon entropy) of real selection patterns across 99 experiments was often lower than in 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations of independent card choices. This refutes theories that treat each card as an independent guess.
numbers: 99 experiments that recorded all 16 selection frequencies. Splitting one experiment at random 10,000 times never gave two subsets that were both more informative than their independent simulations. Nine theories fail to predict dependence.
limits: The authors use entropy, not correlations. Kellen and Klauer argue aggregate data cannot show subject-level dependence; the reply agrees on that point but argues the test is still valid.
agent_relevance: Test choices come as coupled sets, not single slips. A check on a chosen test set should ask whether the whole set contains any falsifier, not judge each test alone.

source: Ragni and Johnson-Laird (2020) Explanation or Modeling: a Reply to Kellen and Klauer
finding: Making potential counterexamples salient raises the correct selection. The authors say no finding in the 228 experiments is as large or as robust. Ten rival theories fail to predict it.
numbers: Counterexample salience was one of three main predictions (canonical set, dependence, salience); the support is in Ragni et al. 2018 Table 4. No effect size is given in this reply.
limits: The effect size is only asserted here; the 2018 table was not opened. Salience manipulations vary a lot between studies.
agent_relevance: A prompt step that makes the agent name a concrete counterexample (what would a falsifying instance look like?) is the best-supported lever for the abstract task.

source: Ragni and Johnson-Laird (2020) Explanation or Modeling: a Reply to Kellen and Klauer
finding: Wason (1969) raised the partial-insight and correct selections by making people imagine what could be on the other side of a card. By the end the most common choice was p+q+not-q, then the correct p+not-q. This could not come from independent guessing.
numbers: Final block of Wason (1969): partial insight 53%, correct 31%. Cited as an old result, not re-run here.
limits: Second-hand (reported in the 2020 reply). Small old study; N not given. The authors need this result to rebut the guessing theory.
agent_relevance: A scripted step that forces the agent to imagine the hidden side of each option may move it from a confirming test to a falsifying one within one session.

source: Ragni and Johnson-Laird (2020) Explanation or Modeling: a Reply to Kellen and Klauer
finding: In the repeated selection task (Johnson-Laird and Wason 1970b) nearly everyone starts by choosing q instances, then learns to pick all the not-q instances once they have feedback. People first seek examples, then search exhaustively for counterexamples.
numbers: Reported as 'nearly every participant' in the first study; no counts in this reply.
limits: Second-hand and no numbers. The task has immediate feedback, which the standard task lacks.
agent_relevance: With feedback from a run, a counterexample search appears quickly. This supports letting code run the test and report back, instead of asking the model to judge it in its head.

source: Ragni and Johnson-Laird (2020) Explanation or Modeling: a Reply to Kellen and Klauer
finding: The rival inference-guessing theory (Klauer et al. 2007) explains the 16 selection frequencies with a 10-parameter processing tree and treats about 25 percent of data as guesses. The model theory camp counters that many free parameters can fit a wrong theory.
numbers: Ten free parameters for 16 outcomes. Klauer et al. consign about 25% of data to guessing; Kellen and Klauer say dropping the non-canonical selections excludes 26% of data. Online samples show more odd selections: median information 2.15 bits (face to face) vs 2.67 bits (online), W = 172, p < .0002.
quote: The inference-guessing theory fits the data well, and yet it is wrong.
limits: The theory dispute is not settled by this reply alone; both sides fit the same data.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a model's explanation of why it chose a test. Part of any test choice may be a guess, in models as in people.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: Many 'confirmation bias' results are one heuristic: the positive test strategy. People test cases they expect to have the target property. This is not the same as wanting to confirm, and it often works.
numbers: Review of rule-discovery, four-card, contingency and personality-testing tasks. Formal analysis uses test types (+Htest, -Htest, +Ttest, -Ttest) and expected information.
quote: people tend to test hypotheses by looking at instances where the target property is hypothesized to be present or is known to be present.
limits: Mostly a theoretical analysis plus literature review. Few new experiments. The analysis assumes the stated task structure.
agent_relevance: Do not just tell the agent to 'try to disprove'. Tell it which kind of test can find a falsifier in this task structure.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: Whether a positive test can falsify depends on how the hypothesis sits next to the true rule. If the hypothesis is inside the true rule (Wason's 2-4-6 case), positive tests can never falsify it. If the hypothesis is wider than the truth, positive tests are the only way to find a falsifier. If they overlap, both test types can.
numbers: Figures 1 to 3 give the cells: 'Ambiguous verification' vs 'Conclusive falsification' for each of +Htest and -Htest. In probabilistic settings a verification can be worth more than a falsification, for example for weak hypotheses (z* > .5).
limits: The best test depends on base rates and on the task. People do not know these values; they use the heuristic by default.
agent_relevance: A test selector in code should compute, per candidate test, which hypotheses it separates. A fixed rule such as 'always seek the negative case' is wrong in general.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: The positive-test tendency has been replicated across many rule-discovery tasks. A DAX/MED relabelling of the 2-4-6 feedback (Tweney et al. 1980) made people treat DAX and MED as two hypotheses and test each with positive tests, which found the rule.
numbers: Cited studies: Klayman and Ha 1985, Mahoney 1976/1979, Mynatt et al. 1977/1978, Taplin 1975, Tweney et al. 1980, Wason and Johnson-Laird 1972. No success rates for DAX/MED in this paper.
limits: Second-hand summary of other work. People also test more widely when given enough test opportunities and no time pressure.
agent_relevance: Reframing yes/no feedback as two named rules makes the agent test both. A two-hypothesis framing (rule A and its complement) is cheap to build into a prompt.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: In the four-card problem the default 'matching' response (p and q) is read as a manifestation of the positive test strategy, not as confusion. People seem to need contextual or 'extra logical' information to see when the default fails.
numbers: Qualitative review of Wason 1966/68, Evans and Lynch 1973, Griggs and Cox 1982, Hoch and Tschirgi 1983/85.
limits: Interpretive. The ambiguity of 'if-then' (biconditional reading) is a rival explanation also cited.
agent_relevance: Give the agent context about the purpose of a test (what outcome would change the decision), not only a restatement of the rule.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection
finding: Across 13 studies (34 abstract selection tasks, 845 subjects) the card selection order was p > q > not-q > not-p. The optimal-data-selection model reproduces this order if p and q are assumed rare.
numbers: 13 studies, 34 tasks, 845 subjects. Model has three free parameters P(p), P(q), P(M_I); expected information gain E(Ig). E(Ig) of the not-p card is always zero.
limits: The model needs the 'rarity assumption' (the properties in the rule are rare), which most tasks never test. Critics say it explains frequencies, not individual reasoning.
agent_relevance: A Bayesian test chooser (expected information gain over candidate hypotheses) is a ready, code-able selector for S7. It gives a ranking, not a verdict.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection
finding: In the negations paradigm (rules with a negated antecedent or consequent) the model's expected information gain tracks how often each card was chosen.
numbers: Spearman rho(16) = .92, p < .0001 across four rule types x four cards, from eight studies. Binomial test on pairwise card comparisons: 19 agreements vs 5 disagreements, p < .005. Poorest fit: the rule with a negated antecedent only (NA).
limits: Fit to aggregate frequencies, not individuals. With 16 data points, a good rank correlation is easier to get. Authors say a residual matching tendency may remain.
agent_relevance: Choices that look wrong for deduction can be right for information gain. The agent should rate tests by information gain, not by logic alone.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection
finding: The model predicts that card choice should shift with how many items fit p and q. Kirby (1994) varied set sizes; predicted E(Ig) for the cards changes order between small-set and large-set conditions.
numbers: Table 6 (P(M_I) = .01): Experiment 1 small P set (1/1,001): p 0.746, q 1.311; large P set (1,000/1,001): p 1.372, q 0.911. Experiment 2 used 1/100, 50/100, 90/100 with a similar pattern.
limits: Read from a table; the observed card frequencies in parentheses were not fully checked. Only Kirby's data are used here.
agent_relevance: Test choice should depend on base rates. An agent that ignores how common a property is will choose tests badly.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1995) Information gain explains relevance which explains the selection task
finding: Reply to Sperber, Cara and Girotto (1995): information gain and relevance theory are compatible. The model fits Sperber et al.'s own experiments, so those data do not discriminate the two theories.
numbers: r(14) = .89, p < .0001 between predicted information gain and observed selections in the Sperber et al. conditions. Also cites fits to Evans and Lynch 1973, Griggs and Cox 1983, Manktelow and Evans 1979, Oaksford and Stenning 1992, Pollard 1985, Reich and Ruth 1982.
limits: The authors defending their own model; a reply paper, not a neutral test. Fit to 16 points.
agent_relevance: Two rival accounts (relevance, information gain) predict the same for many designs. An experiment on our agent must pick a design where they differ, or it proves nothing.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Large language models show the human pattern of better performance on realistic than on arbitrary Wason rules. Human performance is low overall, and both humans and models show matching bias.
numbers: Realistic advantage: humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 (all z > 2.2, p < .03). Only marginal for PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2 (z about 1.78, p about .08). Humans and models forced to pick exactly two cards; chance is a random pair. Humans were not above chance overall.
limits: Two-card forced choice, one prompt style. Some models were better on nonsense nouns than arbitrary ones. Human sample is online.
agent_relevance: Our LLM will do better on a familiar permission or safety rule than on an abstract one. Re-describing an abstract check as a concrete rule may help; test this on our own tasks first.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: In people, slower answers are more accurate. Only the slowest humans beat chance, and only on realistic rules.
numbers: Response time predicted accuracy: z = 4.44, p < .001. Slowest 15% (more than 80 s) were above chance on realistic rules and near chance on arbitrary and nonsense rules. A second sample with a performance bonus showed no significant difference in overall performance or content effect.
limits: Time is not a manipulation; it correlates with ability or effort. The slow/fast split was chosen after seeing the long tail.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 in part: more deliberation does not fix the abstract case, and only helps where content gives a handle. Do not assume more reasoning tokens will yield the falsifying test.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Even people practised in logic do poorly on the abstract task. Mathematics education is associated with better abstract performance, but undergraduate maths majors and academic mathematicians scored below 50 percent.
numbers: Below 50% accuracy on the arbitrary task for maths majors and mathematicians (cited from the paper's refs 57 and 58).
limits: Second-hand citation within the paper. No N shown here.
agent_relevance: Expertise in the field does not remove the failure. Expect the same of a strong model when the form is abstract.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Error analysis: humans prefer the two cards that match the rule's terms (matching bias) and often pick both cards for one part of the rule. Models more often give the correct pair and show the content-based facilitation.
numbers: Fig. 9 splits answers into antecedent-true (AT), consequent-true (CT) and consequent-false (CF) choices; the correct answer is AT + CF. The regression detail is in Appendix C.3.2 (not read).
limits: The appendix with the regression was not read.
agent_relevance: Matching bias is a lexical pull toward the words in the rule. Rewriting the rule with the negated cases spelled out may reduce it.

source: Abe et al. (2026) Evaluation of Deontic Conditional Reasoning in LLMs: The Case of Wason's Selection Task
finding: On a new dataset that separates deontic rules (obligation, permission) from descriptive rules, every tested open LLM was better on deontic rules, by 5.0 to 41.2 points depending on model and prompt.
limits: Preprint (March 2026), English templates. CoT did not always help: gemma3-12b fell from 78.7 (few-shot) to 43.8 (CoT).
agent_relevance: The domain effect is large and reproducible in current open models. Chain-of-thought is not a safe fix for test choice.

source: Abe et al. (2026) Evaluation of Deontic Conditional Reasoning in LLMs: The Case of Wason's Selection Task
finding: The authors compare two accounts of LLM error: confirmation bias (pick p and q) vs matching bias (pick cards that lexically match the rule, even when negated). In the cases shown, selections fit matching bias better.
numbers: gpt-oss-20b, zero-shot, deontic rules: p->q: AT 100%, CT 45%, CF 55%. p->not-q: AT 100%, CT 5%, CF 95%. not-p->q: AT 80%, CT 60%, CF 40%. not-p->not-q: AT 90%, CT 10%, CF 90%.
limits: One model's table read in detail; other models are in the appendix. Deontic rules only, so correct answers and matching can coincide (the authors note this).
agent_relevance: Negation changes what a model tests, so check test lists for lexical echoes of the rule. A negation-flipped mutated input (G3) is a good control.

source: Seals and Shalin (2023) Evaluating the Deductive Competence of Large Language Models
finding: Several LLMs solve the standard Wason task poorly. Content and layout (rule at front or back, shuffled content) change antecedent-card selection in ways that differ from humans, and the social-rule advantage is weaker than in people.
numbers: Mixed-effects model: arbitrary vs non-arbitrary content OR = 1.53 [1.23, 1.90], p < .001; shuffled vs realistic OR = 1.30 [1.14, 1.50]; classic vs front format OR = 1.34 [1.15, 1.57]; front vs back OR = 1.29 [1.10, 1.51]; social-rule status not significant; no effect of which LLM. Dasgupta's zero-shot Chinchilla result is quoted as 50% for realistic vs chance for unrealistic.
limits: Older models (2023). The odds ratios describe how often the antecedent card was chosen, not overall accuracy.
agent_relevance: Layout alone moves results (odds ratios of 1.2 to 1.5). Any test of whether the schema helps must hold layout fixed or the effect is noise.

source: Branchini, Bianchi and Burro (2025) Thinking in opposites improves hypothesis testing performance in Wason's rule-discovery task
finding: A short training that asks people to list the properties of the seed triple, name the opposite of each, and use those opposites to build test triples nearly doubled success on Wason's 2-4-6 task. Listing properties alone did nothing.
numbers: N = 180 (60 per condition). Success: thinking in opposites 78.33%, property analysis only 38.33%, no-prompt control 36.66%. chi2(2, N=180) = 27.986, p < .001; the two non-opposite groups did not differ. About 20% solve it on the first attempt in classic versions.
limits: Italian university sample, paper and pencil, up to three attempts, no time limit (about 15 minutes). Training added solution time.
agent_relevance: The strongest intervention found so far for hypothesis testing: for each property of the current best guess, build the opposite case and test it. It is a scripted, code-checkable operator for S7.

source: Branchini, Bianchi and Burro (2025) Thinking in opposites improves hypothesis testing performance in Wason's rule-discovery task
finding: The gain came from less repetition of the same hypothesis and more awareness of the critical ascending-descending dimension, not from testing more triples.
numbers: Number of triples did not increase; the solution came earlier in the opposites condition than in control (F(2, 89) = 5.702, p = .004 for the attempt at which it was found).
limits: Two judges coded flexibility (Cohen's kappa reported). The attempt analysis covers only those who found the rule.
agent_relevance: Count distinct hypotheses tested, not tests. Penalise repeated tests of the same hypothesis.

source: Branchini, Bianchi and Burro (2025) Thinking in opposites improves hypothesis testing performance in Wason's rule-discovery task
finding: Earlier 2-4-6 work shows contrast helps. Presenting 2-4-6 as a counterexample of the experimenter's rule doubled test triples and quadrupled negative feedback. Gale and Ball found the benefit depends on choosing a useful contrast example.
numbers: Rossi et al. 2001: about twice the test triples, more than four times the negative results, rule found in more than 50% on the first attempt. Gale and Ball: 2-4-6 (DAX) with 6-4-2 (MED) about 75% success vs 4-4-4 about 20% and 9-8-1 about 34%.
limits: Second-hand figures quoted in the paper's review. The contrast must be along the dimension that matters; the wrong contrast gave 20 to 34%.
agent_relevance: The contrast item should differ from the guess in one relevant way (a minimal pair). Random counterexamples are not enough.

source: Osman (2007) Can tutoring improve performance on a reasoning task under deadline conditions?
finding: Socratic tutoring improved selection-task performance under deadline and free-time conditions, and the improvement survived a one-day gap. Tutoring changed mostly the handling of the consequent cards.
numbers: Experiment 1 free-time: logical consequent choices about 37% before and 66% after tutoring (read from a garbled table, so approximate). Experiment 2: session x tutoring F(1,58) = 4.05; tutored group improved, t(29) = 2.35; no-tutoring control did not, t(29) = 0.27. Logical antecedent choices stayed flat (about 85%).
limits: Small cells (30 each), student sample, table garbled in the PDF text. Tutoring combined several techniques, so the active ingredient is unknown.
agent_relevance: A short guided question-and-answer on what each card could hide is a trainable fix for people. For the agent, the equivalent is a forced check per option, not a general instruction.

source: Osman (2007) Can tutoring improve performance on a reasoning task under deadline conditions?
finding: Teaching the logic of conditionals does not by itself fix the selection task. Cheng et al. (1986): a logic tutorial helped only arbitrary problems, a deontic-example tutorial only deontic problems, and only the combination helped all versions. A 12-week logic course did not help.
numbers: Standard abstract task: 4% correct (Johnson-Laird and Wason 1970), 46% p+q, 33% p. Deontic versions reach 74% (Griggs and Cox 1982).
limits: Second-hand, from Osman's introduction. Old studies, small N.
agent_relevance: Giving the agent the modus tollens rule in the prompt is not enough. It needs worked examples in both abstract and concrete forms.

source: Osman (2007) Can tutoring improve performance on a reasoning task under deadline conditions?
finding: Common misreadings of the task cause the standard errors: reading 'other side' as 'underside', treating the conditional as a biconditional, or both. Fixing the misreading changes the selections.
numbers: Sources cited, not opened: Gebauer and Laming 1997, Osman and Laming 2001, Stenning and van Lambalgen 1999/2004.
limits: Second-hand. This is a rival explanation to the 'bias' account: people may be answering a different question.
agent_relevance: S1 UNDERSTAND should restate the rule and what is hidden, and check the restatement. A wrong reading of the task looks like a reasoning error.

source: Staller, Sloman and Ben-Zeev (2000) Perspective effects in nondeontic versions of the Wason selection task
finding: Perspective instructions change the selected cards in nondeontic tasks, including one close to Wason's original. Told to look for a violation of one kind, people pick the matching exclusive set. The authors argue this supports domain-general counterexample accounts over domain-specific social-contract theory.
numbers: Experiment 1: 8% chose p and not-q in the 'p and not-q' perspective, none in the other; 10 people chose not-p and q in the other perspective (Fisher exact p = .015). Experiment 3: 50% and 58% chose p and not-q (two problems) vs 3% and 0% in the other perspective; 54% and 31% chose not-p and q vs 0% (p < .0001).
limits: The rules allow biconditional readings, and the not-p and q selection is not correct for the stated rule. Experiment 1 gave only 8% correct, so the effect is on which counterexample is considered.
agent_relevance: What the agent is told to look for sets which tests it builds. Fix the failure to look for (what counts as a violation) before choosing tests.

source: Swann and Giuliano (1987) Confirmatory search strategies in social interaction
finding: In social belief testing, people spontaneously write questions that confirm the belief they are testing. Certainty is the moderator: uncertain testers ask a mix of confirming and disconfirming questions; certain testers ask mostly confirming, tightly constraining questions.
numbers: Experiment 1 about 49 participants (belief x question type F(1,47) = 4.161, p < .05; judges agreed 93%; over 70% of questions were confirmatory or disconfirmatory). Experiment 2 contrasted high and low certainty. Experiment 3: merely entertaining a belief raised the perceived diagnosticity of belief-confirming evidence.
limits: Student samples and social targets. The 'confirmation' may be the positive test of Klayman and Ha; Experiment 3 shows testers see confirming questions as diagnostic.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: bias grows with certainty. The agent's stated confidence can gate tests: after a confident first answer, force a falsifying test.

source: Godoy Avila, Gavino Lazaro and Anarte Ortiz (2008) Estrategias de comprobacion de hipotesis clinicas (Psicothema 20:188-192)
finding: Psychology students testing clinical hypotheses avoided disconfirming information more than they sought confirming information. Making the test raise certainty in the hypothesis increased confirmatory choices. Numeric probability wording and stressing clinical importance had no clear effect.
numbers: N = 206 across groups (base N = 42, numeric N = 40, order-control N = 41). Numeric group: confirming test 25.0%, disconfirming 17.5%, both 45.0%, none 12.5% (chi2(3) = 9.80, p = .02). Importance manipulation chi2(3) = 3.187, p = .364.
limits: Spanish paper read in the original. Students, vignette, not clinicians. The authors admit the manipulations may have been too weak.
agent_relevance: Telling the agent the task is important is unlikely to change its test choice. Changing what each test can show is what matters.

source: Maegherman (2021) Facilitating falsification in legal decision making (doctoral thesis, Maastricht)
finding: Legal professionals do little better on a Wason variant. In a survey of Dutch judges, most chose only the confirming option; about a fifth chose the correct confirming-and-falsifying pair.
numbers: n = 27 judges, told to pick as few options as possible. 40% confirming only; 22.2% correct. Cites Rachlinski (2012): Dutch judges 32% correct on a less abstract variant; typically fewer than 10% on the abstract task.
limits: Very small, self-selected survey sample. The thesis calls the result relatively good for the task. Variant is not the exact card task.
agent_relevance: Domain experts keep the confirming default. Professional training does not replace a built-in falsification step.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-10-20) Wason selection task
finding: Encyclopedia summary: in Wason's study fewer than 10% found the correct answer, replicated in 1993. Performance on non-arbitrary, evolutionarily familiar problems relates more strongly to general intelligence (Kaufman et al. 2011).
numbers: Kaufman et al. 2011: 112 subjects, a 70-item computerised Cosmides and Tooby style task. No numbers for drinking-age facilitation.
limits: Secondary source, used only to place headline numbers. The Kaufman sentence was truncated in the extract I read.
agent_relevance: Ability predicts success on the familiar, concrete form more than the abstract one. Expect model scale to help most on concrete forms.

source: Griggs and Cox (1982) The elusive thematic-materials effect in Wason's selection task (as cited by Osman 2007)
finding: The drinking-age version of the task gave a large facilitation, about 74% correct, far above the abstract task.
numbers: 74% as quoted in Osman (2007)'s introduction. The original was not opened.
limits: Not opened. Later work shows the effect depends on familiar, remembered rules.
agent_relevance: Familiar rules help; abstract ones do not. Same direction as the LLM content effects.

source: Cheng, Holyoak, Nisbett and Oliver (1986) training study (as cited by Osman 2007)
finding: A 12-week introductory logic course did not improve selection-task performance. Logic training helped only abstract versions, permission examples only deontic versions; the combination helped both.
numbers: No figures taken; the summary comes from Osman (2007).
limits: Not opened. Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Teaching abstract rules alone does not transfer. The scaffold should carry concrete test examples next to the rule.

source: Gale and Ball (2009, 2012) contrast-class studies of the 2-4-6 task (as cited by Branchini et al. 2025)
finding: A DAX/MED contrast where the MED exemplar is the reverse of the seed (6-4-2) lifted solution rates to about 75%; unhelpful contrasts (4-4-4, 9-8-1) gave about 20% and 34%.
numbers: Percentages as quoted in Branchini et al. 2025, not from the originals.
limits: Not opened. Exact titles and years not verified.
agent_relevance: A well-chosen contrast item is the key variable, which supports minimal-pair counterexamples.
